summary: Looks at how to make TCP work well for all users, including those on long thin networks, which have high delay and low bandwidth. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: On a mobile data link, the reply from the other end takes a long time to come back, and TCP waits for that reply before sending more. This memo reviews the ways of making TCP cope with that, and lists which ones to use now, which to wait for, and which to avoid. It also notes that a base station can repair a lost packet itself instead of making the sender cut its rate.

questions: what is a long thin network
how to optimize tcp for wireless
why is latency bad for tcp
subtitle: How to make TCP work well on wireless links that are slow to reply and slow to send.

tldr.problem: TCP was designed for wired networks. On a wireless wide-area link, the round trip takes half a second and the data rate is tens of kilobits per second, so TCP's feedback-driven adaptation is far too slow to reach a good rate.
tldr.mechanism: The memo surveys the candidate fixes and recommends a set of them: a larger initial window, fast retransmit and fast recovery, selective acknowledgements, explicit congestion notification, header compression, and a base-station module called SNOOP that repairs lost packets locally.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and reviews work in progress rather than specifying anything. It recommends implementing the well-established mechanisms now, waiting for a few that are not yet stable, and rejecting a few others, and it warns that several of the fixes stop working once the traffic is encrypted.

facts.label: Buffer needed at 2 Mbps and 200 ms

today: RFC 2757 is an Informational memo from January 2000 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a review of proposals rather than a specification, and its recommendation table reflects the state of the work at that time, so it says of several mechanisms that they should be adopted once they are stable rather than that they are ready.

sections.title: What a Long Thin Network Is
sections.content:
RFC 2757 looks at a class of network the authors call a long thin network, an LTN. Wireless wide-area networks are the example. A W-WAN link is typically 4 to 5 times as long as the equivalent for a wireless LAN, where length is measured as the delay times the bandwidth product. An 802.11 network with a round-trip time of about 3 ms and a bandwidth of 1.5 Mbps gives a product of 4500 bits. A W-WAN such as Ricochet, with a round-trip time around 500 ms and a sustained bandwidth of about 24 Kbps, gives roughly 1.5 KB. Third-generation wireless services offering 384 Kbps with a 200 ms round trip give 76.8 Kbits, which is 9.6 KB, larger than the default 8 KB buffer space used by many TCP implementations. So whereas the default buffer space is enough for a wireless LAN, future wireless WANs will operate inefficiently, meaning they will not be able to fill the pipe, unless they override the default value. A third-generation service offering 2 Mbps with 200 millisecond latency requires a 50 KB buffer.

Latency across a link also affects throughput, because the upper bound on TCP throughput is inversely related to the round-trip time. The long latencies also push the limits, and commonly transgress them, for what is acceptable to users of interactive applications.

Satellite links are the other example of a long network, and those are called long fat networks. They are long because their round-trip time is high, 0.5 seconds and more for geosynchronous satellites, though not all satellite links fall in that regime: a round-trip time in a low-earth-orbit satellite network may be as little as a few milliseconds and never extends beyond 160 to 200 ms. Satellite networks are also fat in the sense that they may have high bandwidth, and they may often have a delay times bandwidth product above 64 KBytes, which poses additional problems to TCP. Wireless WANs do not generally show that behaviour, so the document deals only with links that are long thin pipes, and the networks that contain them.

The document's goal is to identify a TCP that works for all users, including users of long thin networks. It started from the working recommendations of the IETF TCP Over Satellite Links working group, and works towards a set of TCP recommendations that are benign in environments that do not require them. It does not give an overview of the API used to access the underlying transport, treating that as an orthogonal issue, and it focuses on the on-the-wire protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: A long thin network is one whose slowest link is slow in both directions: it takes a long time for a reply to come back, and it carries little data. Mobile networks are the clear example, and satellite links are the opposite case, long but fast. The measurement the memo uses is the product of delay and bandwidth, because that is how much data can be in flight before the sender has to stop and wait.

sections.title: The Network Architecture and Its Constraints
sections.content:
One significant difference between long fat networks and long thin networks is the assumption that the wireless WAN link is the last hop to the end user. That allows the assumption that a single intermediate node sees all packets transferred between the wireless mobile device and the rest of the Internet. The architecture considered is: a wireless mobile device, connected via a wireless link, which may in fact comprise several hops at the link layer, to an intermediate node, sometimes referred to as a base station, connected via a wireline link, which in turn interfaces with the landline Internet and millions of legacy servers and web sites.

The memo is not as concerned with paths that include two wireless segments separated by a wired one, which can occur when one mobile device reaches the Internet through an intermediate node and then on to a second mobile device. Quite often, mobile devices connect to a legacy server on the wired Internet. The endpoints of the wireless segment are normally the intermediate node and the mobile device, although the latter may be a wireless router to a mobile network, which is also important and has applications such as disaster recovery.

The target architecture has implications for what can be deployed. An important requirement is that the networking stack on the legacy servers cannot be altered. It would be preferable to change only the stack at the intermediate node, although changing it at the mobile devices is certainly an option and perhaps a necessity.

The memo also sets out assumptions about the radio link, beyond its being a wireless link. The link may present a higher bit error rate than a wireline network because of burst errors and disconnections. The techniques surveyed usually do not address all types of error, so a complete solution should combine the best of all the proposals, but the document concentrates on the typical case of a higher error rate from random errors, which implies longer and more variable delays because of link-layer error corrections and retransmissions, rather than an interruption of service from a handoff or a disconnection, though those are covered too.

Other assumptions: the wireless service may be datagram oriented or a virtual circuit, with switched virtual circuits more common but packet networks starting to appear. Wireless services typically retransmit a frame until it has been acknowledged, and may allow the user to turn that off; GSM allows the Radio Link Protocol to be turned off, and in GSM RLP a frame is retransmitted until the maximum number of retransmissions is reached, after which the operator either disconnects the physical link or resets it, resynchronising the sequence numbers and flushing the transmit and receive buffers, which results in lost data. Some services, such as CDMA IS95-RLP, limit the latency on the wireless link by retransmitting a frame only a couple of times, which decreases the residual frame error rate significantly but does not provide fully reliable link service. The memo assumes that mobile devices do not transmit and receive simultaneously, because doing so increases the cost of the electronics, and that a mobile device usually addresses only one peer, the intermediate node, at any given time.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture the memo draws is a mobile device talking to a base station over the radio, and the base station talking to the rest of the Internet over ordinary wires. That shape matters because it means there is exactly one place in the middle where a fix could be made, and it means the servers on the far side cannot be changed at all. The radio itself is assumed to lose packets at a higher rate than a wire, sometimes in bursts and sometimes through a dropped connection.

sections.title: The Case for TCP
sections.content:
The memo sets out the case against TCP, and the case for it.

Against: TCP is generally recognized not to perform well in the presence of significant levels of non-congestion loss, and TCP's detractors argue that the wireless medium is one such case, and that it is hard enough to fix TCP, so it is easier to start from scratch. TCP has too much header overhead. And by the time the mechanisms are in place to fix it, TCP is very heavy and ill-suited for use by lightweight, portable devices.

In support: it is preferable to continue using the same protocol that the rest of the Internet uses, for compatibility reasons, and any extensions specific to the wireless link may be negotiated. Legacy mechanisms may be reused, for example the three-way handshake. Link-layer forward error correction and automatic repeat request can reduce the error rate such that any losses TCP does see are in fact caused by congestion, which is what modern wireless WAN technologies do. Hand-offs among different technologies are made possible by Mobile IP, but only if the same protocols are used throughout. And given TCP's wealth of research and experience, alternative protocols are relatively immature and the full implications of their widespread deployment are not clearly understood.

Overall, the authors feel that the performance of TCP over long thin networks can be improved significantly, and the rest of the document discusses the mechanisms to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people argued that TCP should be thrown away for mobile links, because it treats a lost packet as a sign of congestion, and on a radio a lost packet usually means noise rather than a crowded link. The authors answer that throwing away TCP loses compatibility with every server on the Internet, and that the radio link can be made reliable enough at its own layer that what TCP still sees really is congestion. So the answer is to keep TCP and repair the parts that misbehave.

sections.title: Why TCP Struggles
sections.content:
A TCP sender adapts its use of bandwidth based on feedback from the receiver. The high latency characteristic of long thin networks implies that TCP's adaptation is correspondingly slower than on networks with shorter delays, and delayed acknowledgements exacerbate the perceived latency on the link. Because TCP grows its congestion window in units of segments, small maximum transmission units slow adaptation even further.

Two features of slow start and congestion avoidance are adversely affected by the wireless medium. Whenever the retransmission timer expires, the sender assumes that the network is congested and invokes slow start, so it is important to minimise the losses caused by corruption and leave only those caused by congestion. And the sender increases its window based on the number of acknowledgements received, whose rate of arrival depends on the round-trip time, which implies long ramp-up times on high latency links; the dependency lasts until the pipe is filled. During slow start the sender increases its window in units of segments, which is why it is important to use an appropriately large maximum transmission unit, which in turn requires link layers with low loss.

Fast retransmit and fast recovery are also relevant. When a sender receives several duplicate acknowledgements, fast retransmit allows it to infer that a segment was lost and to retransmit it without waiting for the full timeout. After a fast retransmit, fast recovery lets the sender transmit at half its previous rate, regulating the growth of its window by congestion avoidance, rather than beginning a slow start again.

In general TCP can increase its window beyond the delay-bandwidth product, but on long thin links the congestion window may remain rather small, less than four segments, for long periods of time, for several reasons. Typical file sizes to be transferred are relatively small, such as web requests, web document objects and email messages, and users of long thin networks are not very willing to carry out large transfers as the response time is so long. If the link has a high error rate, the congestion window tends to stay small. When a long thin network is combined with a highly congested wireline path, congestion losses on the Internet have the same effect. Commonly, operators configure only a small number of buffers per user in their dial-up routers, even as few as three packets. And small socket buffers are often recommended with long thin networks, in order to prevent the retransmission timeout from inflating and to diminish the amount of packets with competing traffic.

A small window effectively prevents the sender from taking advantage of fast retransmits. Efficient recovery from multiple losses within a single window requires NewReno, and on slow paths with no packet reordering, waiting for three duplicate acknowledgements postpones retransmission unnecessarily. The memo recommends implementing fast retransmit and fast recovery, but does not recommend NewReno because of its experimental nature, preferring selective acknowledgements instead.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP decides how much to send based on acknowledgements coming back, so the longer the round trip the slower it climbs to a good rate. On a mobile link it also mistakes a packet lost to radio noise for a sign that the network is busy, and cuts its rate when it should not. And if the window is small, which it often is because the transfers are small and the operator has only a few buffers per user, the sender cannot even use the fast retransmit that would recover a loss quickly.

sections.title: Summary of Recommended Optimizations
sections.content:
The memo ends with a table of recommendations. The first column, stability of the proposal, refers to maturity: an IETF proposal is either an Internet draft or an RFC, a Draft Standard is standards track and carries more weight than a Proposed Standard which may still undergo revisions, and Informational or Experimental RFCs do not specify a standard. The implemented-at column says which participant in a TCP session must be modified to implement the proposal, using WS for the wireless sender, WR for the wireless receiver, WD for the wireless device, IN for the intermediate node and NI for the network infrastructure. Legacy servers typically cannot be modified, so the column indicates whether implementation happens at either or both of the two nodes under some control, the mobile device and the intermediate node.

Recommended for immediate adoption are an increased initial window, following RFC 2581 with an initial window of 2 segments; TCP header compression for PPP, following RFC 1144; IP payload compression, following RFC 2393, which is also needed on the server; header compression following RFC 2507 and RFC 2509, for IPv4, TCP and Mobile IP over PPP; SNOOP plus selective acknowledgements, with SNOOP in limited use; fast retransmit and fast recovery, which the memo says should be there already; explicit congestion notification, following RFC 2481; and tracking the research on TCP control block interdependence.

Recommended when stable are disabling delayed acknowledgements during slow start, delayed duplicate acknowledgements, and class-based queuing on end systems. Not recommended are byte counting instead of acknowledgement counting, transaction-oriented TCP, and estimating the slow start threshold.

The memo notes that of all the optimizations in the table, only SNOOP plus selective acknowledgements and delayed duplicate acknowledgements are currently being proposed only for wireless networks, the others being considered even for non-wireless applications, which attracts more attention and analysis from the research community. Of the mechanisms listed, only header compression for IP and TCP and SNOOP plus selective acknowledgements cease to work in the presence of IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The final table is the practical output of the document. For each candidate fix it says how settled the idea is, where in the system the change has to be made, and whether to use it now, use it once it has settled down, or leave it alone. The changes that work in any network are preferred, because they attract more study and are more likely to be implemented everywhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms discussed and recommended have been proposed in previous publications, so the security considerations outlined in the original discussions apply here as well, and the memo says several security issues are also discussed throughout the document. It then lists the most salient issues concerning the recommended mechanisms.

A larger initial TCP window size has no known security issues. Header compression may be open to some denial of service attacks, but any attacker in a position to launch these attacks would have much stronger attacks at his disposal. Congestion control, fast retransmit and fast recovery can be abused: an attacker may force TCP connections to grind to a halt, or, more dangerously, behave more aggressively, which may lead to congestion collapse at least in some regions of the network. Explicit congestion notification does not appear to increase the vulnerabilities in the network, and may reduce them by aiding the identification of flows unresponsive to or non-compliant with TCP congestion control.

Sharing of network performance information, through TCP control block sharing and the Congestion Manager module, raises its own problem: some information should not be shared, because TCP sequence numbers are used to protect against spoofing attacks, and even limiting the sharing to performance values leaves open the possibility of denial of service attacks.

Performance enhancing proxies are men in the middle from the point of view of their security vulnerabilities, and must be used with extreme care so as to prevent their being hijacked and misused. The memo says this point is not to be underestimated: there is a general security concern whenever an intermediate node performs operations different from those carried out on an end-to-end basis. In particular, there may be a tendency to forego IPsec-based privacy in order to allow, for example, a SNOOP module, header compression or HTTP proxies to work. Adding end-to-end security at higher layers, for example by encrypting the TCP payload with TLS, alleviates the problem, but this still leaves protocol headers in the clear, and these may be exploited for traffic analysis and denial of service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of the recommended fixes work by having the base station look inside the traffic, which conflicts with encrypting it. The memo says this is the general risk whenever a machine in the middle does something the end points would otherwise do, and it warns that operators may be tempted to drop encryption to make a fix work. Encrypting the payload at a higher layer helps, but the headers stay readable, and those can be used to work out who is talking to whom.

viz.caption: THE RECOMMENDATION TABLE IN BRIEF (RFC 2757 SECTION 5)

items.title: Increased initial window
items.text: Adopt now, with an initial window of 2 segments.

items.title: Fast retransmit and recovery
items.text: Adopt now; it should already be there.

items.title: Selective acknowledgements
items.text: Adopt now, especially together with SNOOP.

items.title: Header compression
items.text: Adopt now for IP, TCP and Mobile IP over PPP.

items.title: SNOOP
items.text: Adopt now; the base station repairs losses locally.

items.title: Disable delayed acknowledgements
items.text: Wait until the mechanism is stable.

items.title: Transaction-oriented TCP
items.text: Do not use; it is experimental and has security problems.
